source: Benjamin (2019) Errors in probabilistic reasoning and judgment biases, Handbook of Behavioral Economics chapter (NBER w25200)
finding: Across dozens of bookbag-and-poker-chip experiments, people update less than Bayes' rule says (underinference, once called conservatism). Overinference is rare. Edwards' urn example: intuitive answer 70-80%, correct 97%.
numbers: Edwards (1968) example: 8 red of 12 draws, 70/30 urns, equal priors; likelihoods 0.231 vs 0.008; correct posterior 97%. Regression of subjective on normative log-odds ratio in the pooled data of Fig 2A: slope c-hat = 0.20 (SE 0.063). Mean c-hat for samples of size 2-6: 0.73, 0.98, 0.52, 1.06, 0.67 (SE 0.07-0.10).
quote: Underinference is by far the dominant direction of bias.
limits: Stylized Fact 1. Overinference appears when the two signal rates are close (e.g. 0.6 vs 0.5) and in a few studies (Peterson and Miller 1965; Grether 1992 Study 2). Sample sizes 3 and 5 cannot reject overinference.
agent_relevance: A human-like model may under-move on evidence. Code-side Bayes with explicit likelihoods avoids the human pattern; do not copy human cautious updating.

source: Benjamin (2019) Errors in probabilistic reasoning and judgment biases, Handbook of Behavioral Economics chapter (NBER w25200)
finding: Underinference gets worse as the sample grows (people treat 8:4 and 40:20 as nearly the same). The reported belief follows the sample proportion, not the count difference.
numbers: Kahneman and Tversky card-deck problem (proportion 2/3): median reported belief 70% for 8a/4b (correct 94%), 68% for 4a/2b (correct 80%), 70% for 40a/20b (correct 99.9999%).
limits: Stylized Facts 2 and 4. Hypothetical one-shot questions; incentives vary across studies.
agent_relevance: Many small pieces of evidence are under-weighted. In S7, count independent passes explicitly in code rather than asking the model how strong the evidence is overall.

source: Benjamin (2019) Errors in probabilistic reasoning and judgment biases, Handbook of Behavioral Economics chapter (NBER w25200)
finding: People under-use prior (base-rate) information too. Complete neglect is common in some vignettes but the typical result is partial under-use. Underinference and base-rate neglect are not in conflict.
numbers: Kahneman and Tversky engineer-lawyer problem: 30% vs 70% engineers in the pool gave mean probability 50% vs 55%, odds ratio about 1.2 versus the Bayesian 5.4. Cab problem (85% blue, witness 80% accurate): correct 41%; only about 10% of Bar-Hillel's high-school respondents were close; modal answer 80% (36% of respondents).
limits: Bar-Hillel (1980): neglect shrinks when base rates are causal or specific (85% of accidents involve blue cabs) or when the likelihood is made as weak as the base rate (intercom variant). Replicated with 99%/1% base rates, law students (Eide 2011), 988 Germans (Dohmen 2009) and incentivised markets (Ganguly, Kagel, Moser 2000).
agent_relevance: When S7 combines a class pass-rate with a check result, show both as counts in one table and let code multiply. Causal framing of the prior reduces neglect in people.

source: Benjamin (2019) Errors in probabilistic reasoning and judgment biases, Handbook of Behavioral Economics chapter (NBER w25200)
finding: Feedback with the correct posterior can remove underinference within a few dozen trials, but the correction does not transfer cleanly.
numbers: Martin and Gettys (1969): posterior feedback gave less underinference than true-state feedback, but no detectable learning over 200 trials. Donnell and DuCharme (1975): posterior feedback after each of 60 problems eliminated underinference, nearly all in the first 10 trials; on a new problem where naive people infer correctly, trained people then overinferred.
limits: Few studies. Small laboratory samples. Overshoot suggests a shift in response scale, not a better model.
agent_relevance: A fixed confidence correction can overshoot on a new class; fit corrections per class from our own run records and keep them in code.

source: Benjamin (2019) Errors in probabilistic reasoning and judgment biases, Handbook of Behavioral Economics chapter (NBER w25200)
finding: In sequential updating people do not pool signals as Bayes' rule does. Recent signals count more. Updating itself seems to trigger base-rate neglect.
numbers: Stylized Facts 8-11. Troutman and Shanteau (1977): even uninformative signals moved beliefs. Benjamin, Bodoh-Creed, Rabin (2018) model: posterior odds = likelihood ratio x prior odds^d with 0<d<1, so older signals fade as d^k.
limits: Model is a fit; primacy appears in some designs, recency in others.
agent_relevance: Order effects are the human signature. For an LLM agent, test order sensitivity directly: shuffle the order of checks and see whether code-normalised probabilities change (they should not).

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs do not update like a Bayesian assistant on a five-round preference task. Accuracy stalls after one round. Fine-tuning on a Bayesian assistant's outputs (not on the truth) fixes this and transfers to other domains.
numbers: Models: Gemma 2 (9B, 27B), Llama 3 (8B, 70B), Qwen 2.5 (7B, 32B), Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4.1 Mini. Bayesian-tuned models agree with the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time; simulated-user accuracy after 5 rounds near 80%. Human users, N=500: original LLM baseline 37.0% (flights); Oracle-tuned +24.0 points; Bayesian-tuned +38.5 points (95% CI 31.1-45.9). Hotel: baseline 36.7%, Oracle +16.7, Bayesian +29.4. Web shopping: baseline 54.0%, Oracle +7.1, Bayesian +18.6.
quote: LLMs' performance often plateaus after a single interaction
limits: Training, not scaffolding. Tuned only at 7-9B. Simulated users are simple. Human assistants (N=720) improved from round 1 to 5 (p=0.002). A gap to the Bayesian assistant persists. Web-shopping transfer stays below direct tuning; the Qwen family dropped 11.1 points on web shopping.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that a model's own in-context updating is weak, so the Bayes computation in S7 should live in code. We cannot fine-tune.

source: Gupta et al. (2025) Enough Coin Flips Can Make LLMs Act Bayesian
finding: On biased coin flips and dice, open models start from wrong priors but, once shown enough flips in context, follow Bayesian posteriors. Most error comes from the prior, not the update. In-context evidence beats a stated bias instruction.
numbers: Non-instruct models put about 60-80% on heads regardless of the stated bias; metric is total variation distance over 50 prompt variants. Instruction-tuned models follow bias statements better. Model size (Pythia 70M-12B) has negligible effect on updating. Instruct models update more locally (shorter memory) than base models. Attention magnitude had little effect.
quote: deviations primarily due to miscalibrated priors rather than flawed updates
limits: Models 2B-8B (Gemma-2, Phi, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, OLMoE), token-probability readout renormalised over outcomes, one trivial task. Authors do not claim the models are Bayesian.
agent_relevance: Supports letting code do the update and treating model-stated priors as untrusted. Renormalising over a fixed outcome set is the same step as G5.

source: Falck et al. (2024) Is In-Context Learning in Large Language Models Bayesian? A Martingale Perspective
finding: A Bayesian predictor on exchangeable data must satisfy the martingale property. Several LLMs violate it, so their in-context updating is not coherent Bayesian updating, and order matters.
numbers: Bernoulli (n=50, theta 0.3/0.5/0.7): short paths mostly within reference intervals, GPT-4 off at theta 0.3 and 0.5; long paths (m=2n) deviate more often. Gaussian (theta=-1, n=100, m=50): all models violate except gpt-3.5. Synthetic clinical text task (n=80, m=40): gpt-3.5 and gpt-4 deviate. llama-2-7b and gpt-3.5 shrink uncertainty more slowly than Bayes; gpt-3.5 is overconfident with small samples.
limits: Small synthetic tasks; outliers removed; GPT-4 used in a subset; older models (llama-2-7B, mistral-7B, GPT-3, 3.5, 4).
agent_relevance: Do not ask the model to hold a running posterior across turns. Recompute from the full evidence table each time, and test with a shuffle check.

source: Zhu and Griffiths (2024) Eliciting the Priors of LLMs using Iterated In-Context Learning
finding: GPT-4 chains behave like a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler from the model's prior. Elicited priors look like human priors in several domains. Direct prompting for priors often yields refusals or broad ranges.
numbers: 100 chains of 12 iterations at temperature 1. Causal strength (generative): Pearson r = 0.86, RMSD 0.19 for the empirical prior vs 0.85/0.21 uniform and 0.79/0.25 sparse-strong. Preventive: r = 0.79 best, but uniform had lowest RMSD (0.26 vs 0.27). Chains converged by iteration 7-8. Median years: 2042 superhuman AI, 2045 zero carbon, 2050 Mars colony.
limits: Human comparison is by visual inspection, no formal test. The assumption that an LLM is an approximate Bayesian agent is untested. Does not test base-rate neglect.
agent_relevance: LLM priors are inspectable but unreliable; for S7 use frequencies from our own run records as priors, not the model's stated prior.

source: LLMs are not (consistently) Bayesian: quantifying internal (in)consistencies of LLMs' probabilistic beliefs (arXiv 2605.06915; authors not recorded)
finding: The paper elicits a model's own prior and likelihood, computes the Bayes posterior from them, and measures the gap to the model's stated posterior as KL divergence. Batch updates (all evidence at once) are much further from Bayes than step-by-step belief propagation. Reasoning models are close to Bayes step by step.
numbers: Models: Qwen3 8B/14B, Ministral 8B/14B (reasoning and not), DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B, GPT-4o mini, GPT-5.1 (medium and none). Four multiple-choice datasets: Animals, Political Ideology, MediQ, Eleusis. GPT-5.1 is 'very close to optimal' in step mode but 'frequently far from optimal' in batch mode. About half of wrong-direction batch updates match a GPT-5.1-derived oracle likelihood; about 15% more contradict both likelihoods yet land nearer the oracle posterior.
limits: Gap measure not comparable across steps or datasets; depends on elicitation format; multiple-choice only. On MediQ all models would do worse if made explicitly Bayesian; on Eleusis most would do better, but strong reasoning models would do worse.
agent_relevance: Key warning for S7: being more Bayesian is not always better, because the model's own likelihoods can be wrong. Prefer step-by-step updates over one-shot posteriors, and score the update rule on held-out class records.

source: Filbry, Melo, Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context? (arXiv 2610.29331)
finding: Without tools LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule when updating in context. With reasoning and code execution they get close to the analytic posterior, even for intractable ones. Non-Bayesian updates cost real task success.
numbers: Coherence: 10 ForecastBench scenarios per violation type (normalisation, monotonicity, extensionality) for 3 models (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemma-4-31B-it, Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct). Across separate conversations, violation rates exceed 50% of 30 scenarios for almost all model-axiom pairs; within one dialogue about 10% (Gemini) and 1 of 30 (Gemma). Sequential updating without reasoning: posterior mass gap to the oracle at least 30% across all models. Gemma-4-31B, one experiment, no reasoning: 0.643 on the right class where the oracle gives 0.967; with reasoning it matched the oracle. With code, Gemini-2.5-Pro KL and gap approach 0 on ProteinWorld-hard.
quote: LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule when updating their beliefs in context.
limits: Small samples (40 runs per environment). The 20-Questions oracle uses the LLM's own likelihoods, so it tests internal consistency only. Reasoning on/off only. Preprint, October 2026.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G5: do normalisation and posterior arithmetic in code. Normalisation violations across separate calls above 50% mean probabilities from separate calls must be renormalised by code.

source: Large Language Models as Discounted Bayesian Filters (arXiv 2512.18489; authors not recorded)
finding: LLM sequence predictions are fit by a Bayesian filter that tempers old evidence by gamma<1. The fitted gamma is below 1 for all models, and instruct-tuned models discount more. Most error is model misspecification, not the update rule.
numbers: Tasks: biased die and Gaussian mean, T=100 with change point at t=51 (mean 2.0 to -2.0). Models: base and instruct Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-2B. Update divergence typically under 13% of total error. Llama-3.1-8B on the die: attention to past evidence correlates with step-wise update divergence at rho = -0.85.
limits: Models 2B-8B; two probe tasks; correlational attention result; gamma values only in a figure.
agent_relevance: A forgetting parameter is an explainable deviation. In a long agent run, older check results may fade; keep the evidence table in code so nothing fades.

source: Vision-Language Models Integrate Conflicting Evidence Like Biased Bayesian Observers (arXiv 2610.19407; authors not recorded)
finding: When text and image disagree, a VLM's preference between answers is well described as additive log-odds with unequal weights per modality plus a prior. No interaction term is needed.
numbers: 2,765 examples (DocVQA 1,000, VQAv2 1,000, RealworldQA 765); 6 blur levels x 6 text-noise levels. Out-of-distribution R^2: 0.852 Qwen2.5-VL, 0.800 Qwen3.5, 0.692 Gemma3, 0.860 GLM-4.6V. Unit-weight naive Bayes only 0.477-0.717. Weight ratio text/vision 0.56-0.68 for Qwen3.5 and GLM, 0.96-1.27 for Gemma3. Qwen3.5 prior weight 0.53-0.66. Cross-modal interaction adds at most 0.001 R^2.
limits: Models 3-4B; weights fitted, not derived; preferences from length-normalised log-likelihood, not generation; prior never manipulated independently.
agent_relevance: Evidence from different sources is combined additively but with unequal, model-specific weights. Fit per-source weights from our own records rather than setting all to 1.

source: Feng, Zhou, Lin, Roth (2025) BIRD: A Trustworthy Bayesian Inference Framework for LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: The LLM only proposes factors and gives coarse labels; a learned Bayesian network computes the probabilities. These agree with human preference far better than the LLM's direct ones and give better decisions on hard sets.
numbers: F1 of 59% for both base models, 'more than 30% higher than GPT-4' on human-judged pairwise probability comparison. Training uses 128 complete-information instances per scenario and 7 coarse levels (0%, 20%, ... 100%). Abductive factor generation beat direct factor generation by 4.4 / 3.9 points accuracy (Llama-2 / Llama-3.1). Beat CoT with self-consistency using Llama-3.1 on all decision benchmarks; comparable with Llama-2; clearest gain on the hardest set (TODAY).
limits: Instances whose factors cannot be mapped are dropped (fallback to CoT assumed). Probability estimation differs from hard-label classification: CoT sometimes wins through spurious cues. Needs per-scenario training.
agent_relevance: A hybrid: model proposes hypotheses and features, code owns the table and the arithmetic. Matches the S7 design.

source: Arora, Jurafsky, Potts, Goodman (2025) Bayesian scaling laws for in-context learning
finding: A law derived from an ideal Bayesian learner fits the ICL curve as well as or better than power-law baselines on GPT-2 toys and real LLMs (1B-405B), with interpretable prior, efficiency and per-example terms. Post-training mostly shifts the prior over tasks, not task knowledge, so many-shot ICL can bring suppressed behaviour back.
numbers: Real LLMs: 7 instruction-tuned Gemma and Llama models, 1B to 405B; 2 multiple-choice reasoning sets, 3 binary-choice personality sets, 1 new many-shot jailbreak set (HarmBench); 50 many-shot prompts per dataset-model pair. Toy: GINC data, fine-tuning on 1% to 100% of 5 epochs of pretraining data; DPO with 0.1% to 10%.
limits: Good fit is not proof of a Bayesian mechanism; with enough DPO the fit error rises for all laws. Toy results are on synthetic HMMs.
agent_relevance: Evidence in the prompt shifts output like a prior update; a rule stated in a system prompt can be overridden by enough contrary examples. Do not rely on a prompt-stated prior against many contrary observations.

source: Zhao, Wallace, Feng, Klein, Singh (2021) Calibrate Before Use: Improving Few-Shot Performance of Language Models
finding: Few-shot accuracy swings widely with prompt format, example choice and order. The model is biased toward the majority label, the last example and common tokens. Dividing by the output for a content-free input (N/A) removes much of this.
numbers: Changing example order in sentiment analysis moved GPT-3 from 54% to 93%. Contextual calibration improved mean and worst-case accuracy by up to 30.0 points absolute; GPT-3 2.7B beat the 175B baseline by up to 19.3 points. Variance did not shrink with more examples or larger models.
limits: GPT-3 and GPT-2 era; classification-style tasks; calibration reduces but does not remove variance.
agent_relevance: A label-bias correction for the model's answer position before its probabilities are used as likelihoods in S7.

source: Paruchuri et al. (2024) What Are the Odds? Language Models Are Capable of Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: LLMs estimate percentiles, draw samples and compute probabilities for known distributions better than expected; examples, real-world context or a simplified Normal assumption help even when the assumption is wrong.
numbers: Models: Gemini 1.0 Ultra, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 Turbo; 12 idealised distributions. Percentile zero-shot MAE 16.52% on average (best 0.54% uniform, 2.29% normal); probabilities MAE 21.48% (range 9.03-32.53); sampling poor. Percentile MAE by model: GPT-3.5 25.7, GPT-4 Turbo 14.9, Gemini Ultra 16.5. Within-distribution one-shot improved percentiles by +59.14%, sampling +55.26% (K-S), probabilities +70.13%.
limits: Older models; error in percentage points of probability mass; not a belief-updating test.
agent_relevance: Computing from a stated distribution is within reach but not reliable zero-shot; compute probabilities in code.

source: Mandel, Karvetski, Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails? JDM 13(6)
finding: Making analysts' probabilities over exclusive options sum to one (coherentisation) cut error, and averaging after that cut it further. Plain normalisation did about as well as the more elaborate coherentisation.
numbers: From the project's earlier claim file (fetch of the page failed this session): error down about 35% from coherentisation; about 61% after averaging; 50 analysts.
limits: Human analysts, one task; LLM transfer untested; numbers taken from earlier project notes, not re-read here.
agent_relevance: Already behind G5; adds no new weight. Normalisation is the cheap part of conditionalization with direct evidence of benefit.

source: Schulz, Wegwarth, Giese (2025) Risk expression using likelihood ratios and natural frequencies in Bayesian inference tasks (BMC Med Educ), preregistered crossover RCT
finding: Natural frequencies still help for a single test but most students still fail, and for two sequential tests the odds/likelihood-ratio format did better.
numbers: N=329 completed (167 medical, 162 psychology students). Single test: 36.2% correct with natural frequencies vs 21.6% with odds/LR, OR 2.41. Two tests: 4.9% vs 10.6%, OR 2.73 favouring odds/LR. Natural-frequency advantage not significant in psychology students (OR 1.45, p=0.22); OR 1.74 with no prior exposure. Odds/LR advantage vanished with prior exposure (OR 0.83). The paper cites the McDowell and Jacobs meta-analysis: 76% still fail the PPV.
limits: German students only; binary scoring; conditional independence assumed for sequential tests.
agent_relevance: A format that helps a one-step update can hurt chained updates. Use counts for a single update and odds ratios for chaining; keep chaining in code.

source: Feufel et al. (2023) Boosting for insight and/or for agency? How to maximize accurate test interpretation with natural frequencies (BMC Med Educ)
finding: Natural frequencies and a one-hour training effect are additive. Together they bring medical students to 89% correct.
numbers: N=577 fifth-year medical students, pre/post. Conditional probabilities pretest 36%; natural frequencies pretest 68% (OR 11.55, 95% CI 7.92-16.87); conditional probabilities after training 64% (OR 8.53); natural frequencies after training 89% (OR 21.5 vs all others). Interaction OR 0.98, p=0.759. 30% improved on the probability task after training; 1.4% got worse.
limits: No control group; same two items before and after; no follow-up; classroom setting.
agent_relevance: Format and instruction add up. Give the agent counts (natural frequencies) and a worked step, not conditional probabilities.

source: Cui, Lo, Liu (2023) The Use of Visualizations to Improve Bayesian Reasoning: A Literature Review (Vision 7(1))
finding: Natural frequencies and icon arrays raise Bayesian accuracy in many studies, but results are mixed and the mechanism is unresolved.
numbers: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995): 48% correct with frequencies vs 22% with probabilities. Binder et al. (2015): 42% vs 5%; no visuals 26% vs 2%; with visuals 51% vs 6%. Garcia-Retamero and Hoffrage (2013): 51% vs 38%. Physicians: 46% vs 10%. Children grades 4-6: 0% with probabilities, 19/39/53% with frequencies. Kurzenhauser and Hoffrage (2002): frequency-tree training almost 3x more accurate than rule training after two months. Null or mixed: Wu et al. (2017), Khan et al. (2015; only 20% solved the mammography problem), Zikmund-Fisher 2014, Gaissmaier 2012, Sirota 2014.
limits: Review is not exhaustive and notes publication bias. Individual differences matter (numeracy, spatial ability).
agent_relevance: Representation changes performance more than slogans do. Present evidence as 'out of N cases, k passed' tables.

source: Mellers and McGraw (1999), Yamagishi (2003), Sirota et al. (2015), Brase (2021) as summarised in Cui et al. (2023)
finding: Rival accounts of why natural frequencies help: nested sets (visible set structure), ecological rationality (frequency is the natural format), and problem interpretation (mental representation). Experiments have not cleanly separated them.
numbers: Yamagishi (2003): frequency format had only a mild effect, and roulette wheels beat tree diagrams. Sirota et al. (2015) favour problem interpretation. Brase and Hill (2017): pictures plus frequencies performed best; interaction terms explained only 8% of variance.
limits: Secondary report; effect sizes not given for these contrasts.
agent_relevance: Do not build a theory on frequency prompting; test the table format on our own tasks.

source: Do Chains-of-Thoughts of LLMs Suffer from Hallucinations, Cognitive Biases, or Phobias in Bayesian Reasoning? (arXiv 2503.15268; authors not recorded)
finding: Gemini Flash 2.0, o3-mini and DeepSeek R1 reached correct final answers on one Bayesian problem but often with flawed reasoning, and defaulted to symbolic probability formulas instead of natural frequencies even when asked.
numbers: One problem, three models, one run each (Gemini twice on prompt 1), four prompt stages. Reasoning length 204 to 8,457 words; time 10 to 625 seconds. Longer chains had more doubt but not more accuracy. Prompting for frequencies, blocks and colours raised use of the formats but not reliability.
limits: No accuracy statistics; one coder; one date; the training-data explanation is untested.
agent_relevance: A correct stated answer does not prove a correct update. Verify arithmetic by code, not by reading the reasoning.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Bayesian Epistemology (conditionalization sections)
finding: Conditionalization sets the probability of what the evidence excludes to zero and rescales the rest, so ratios among the survivors stay fixed. Support: Dutch-book arguments (Lewis 1999, Teller 1973) and accuracy-dominance arguments (Briggs and Pettigrew 2020). Main objection read in this session: old evidence (Glymour, Earman).
numbers: Rule: Cr'(X) = Cr(X and E) / Cr(E), with Cr(E) not 0. No numbers. Only the first part of the entry was read (to section 5.1); forgetting, self-locating and higher-order evidence sections were not read.
limits: The rule cannot move a credence of 0 or 1 and gives no verdict on credence change without new evidence. Dutch-book support is a practical, not an epistemic, reason.
agent_relevance: A candidate eliminated by a hard check goes to zero and cannot return; use hard zeroing only for deterministic, correct checks (G3), otherwise a soft update.

source: Benjamin (2019) Errors in probabilistic reasoning and judgment biases, Handbook of Behavioral Economics chapter (NBER w25200)
finding: Rival explanations for underinference: wrong beliefs about sampling distributions (too flat), conservatism proper, and biased use of priors. The sampling-distribution account fails for single-signal updates, where people still underinfer.
numbers: Section 5: Edwards' model has a parameter beta where the subjective sampling distribution is flatter than the true one; for symmetric signal rates beta equals c. Benjamin, Rabin, Raymond (2016) NBLLN model reflects too-flat sampling beliefs and sample-size neglect. Stylized Fact 3 (mean underinference after a single signal) cannot be explained by that theory unless people misjudge a known single-draw rate.
limits: Theory section; no direct test of single-draw beliefs is cited.
agent_relevance: No strong theory exists; treat the model's update error as unexplained and measure it per class.
